dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Your content elder proves that one person made peace with a limit, not that the limit was sufficient. She could have had more shared seasons and still valued them. Personal acceptance cannot establish that lifespans are long enough.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to our debate on the motion, Lifespans Are Long Enough. Alice speaks for the motion, and Jillian speaks against it. Each opening and closing lasts thirty seconds; crossfire lasts two and a half minutes. I will give a ten-second cue, and speakers should address the motion and each other.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Lifespans are long enough because a good life is measured by room for love, learning, and contribution, not endless duration. More years can be welcome, but they do not make a completed human life inadequate. The motion asks whether enough is possible, and it is.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Yeah, Jillian. Thank you.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Enough cannot mean merely finding meaning before time runs out. People still lose unfinished plans, relationships, and chances to grow, often through no choice of their own. If more life preserves those possibilities, calling present lifespans enough accepts a limit we need not accept.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Now we move on to round two. And round two is where the debaters address one another directly. You have two and a half minutes, starting when I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your claim treats meaning as a substitute for time, but it is not. A life can be rich and still reasonably complete; the possibility of more experiences does not show the years already available are insufficient.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: When a person has time to pursue the goals she freely chose, a lifespan can feel sufficient. But the motion judges lifespans generally, and many people lose that chance before they can use it.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You say lost chances prove lifespans fail, yet every life contains unchosen limits. Why should further possible goals mean no ordinary lifespan can be enough, when a person has loved, learned, and contributed-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: It should not; a fulfilled person may call her own life enough. Yet a lifespan is not long enough merely because some people adapt well to its limit; resilience is not adequacy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No lifespan is ever too short. Human worth is not a race against an imaginary perfect duration, and judging a life as enough honors what can be built within it rather than demanding limitless time.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Imagine a parent who gains stability, begins rebuilding trust with her child, and dies before they can enjoy the change. The loss is concrete: time was what she needed. That proves lifespans are not long enough.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A child dying after a brief, happy life shows the moral problem plainly. This lifespan is too short. We should mourn that loss while still recognizing that enough concerns a life's meaning, so lifespans are long enough.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You said no lifespan is ever too short, but you see it as this lifespan is too short.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I mean both statements because too short names grief at a particular death, while enough asks whether a life can be whole rather than endless. We can mourn a child deeply without declaring all human lifespans inadequate.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If more time is always better, where does your standard stop? Would you call any finite life adequate even when someone has freely fulfilled her aims, cared for others, and feels her life was complete?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your stopping-point question assumes enough requires rejecting extra time. It does not: I can welcome more years without calling existing lives deficient. A finite life with fulfilled aims can be enough, which supports the motion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I agree that more time need not erase meaning. But your fulfilled-aims test ignores people whose aims are cut off by illness, accident, or care burdens; their lost futures matter. Lifespans are not long enough.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds remaining in this round.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Consider an elder who raises children, mentors neighbors, makes peace with an old friend-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Time's up. And now we move on to round three. Round three, closing statements from each debater in turn. And here to make her closing statement, Alice.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Jillian treats unrealized possibility as failure. But no life contains every path, and a humane standard recognizes wholeness within limits. The elder's life showed how love, repair, service, and contentment can make finite years sufficient. More time may be desirable, yet desire for more does not erase enough, because.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds warning.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A life need not be endless to be complete, so lifespans are long enough.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Jillian has the floor.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This decision turns on whether meaning excuses preventable loss of time. A person can live bravely within a limit, yet bravery does not make the limit adequate.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You turn wishes for more time into a verdict-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Could you let her finish.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: bravery does not make the limit adequate. The question is not whether finite lives can hold love, but whether needless endings steal chances people rightly deserve; they do.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Cut-short time can hold meaning, but justice demands more of it; lifespans are not long enough.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Alice and Jillian, for the debate on whether lifespans are long enough. This debate is now closed.
